Once you see The Thing on the Doorstep as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Daniel Upton, the story's narrator, explains that he has killed his best friend, Edward Derby, and that he hopes his account will prove that he is not a murderer. Derby had been interested in the occult even as a very young boy, which led to him befriending Upton.

The story The Thing on the Doorstep tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Whenever Derby visited he always used the same knocking pattern of three strokes, a pause, and then two additional strokes on the knocker; Upton had always been able to identify Derby this way. Derby's parents had always doted on him and he had a particular reliance on them, especially his mother.

The honest version of The Thing on the Doorstep starts by giving up the comforting part. Occasionally he is driven back by a chauffeur or mechanic while he huddles in the back seat of the car. One night he comes to Upton's door in a panic and proclaims how he will never let her do a certain thing to him again.

Strip The Thing on the Doorstep of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Derby tries to hint at how he believes that Asenath's late father, Ephraim Waite, may not actually be dead. In the midst of this story he abruptly stops, as if some hypnotic spell has come over him.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — The Thing on the Doorstep shows exactly where that breaks. Upton is later called to pick up Derby, who has been found in Chesuncook, Maine, rambling incoherently. On the trip back, Derby tells of Asenath using his body, and is certain that it is in fact Ephraim who resides in the body of Asenath.

What looks like free choice in The Thing on the Doorstep is older than choice itself. However, Upton sees a change in his eyes; he thinks they look like Asenath's eyes, then that they look perhaps more like Ephraim's eyes. A few months later, Derby shows up at Upton's door and says he has found a way to keep Asenath away and to stop her from using his body, implying some sort of spell or ritual.

Nobody designed the part of The Thing on the Doorstep you experience — it was inherited. Derby finishes renovations on his old family home yet seems strangely reluctant to leave the Crowninshield House. Upton receives another visit from Derby, who begins raving about his wife and father-in-law and how he can still feel her, him, it, clawing at his mind while he sleeps, trying to get hold of him.

Every serious account of The Thing on the Doorstep eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Upton gets Derby to sleep, but then has him taken to a sanitarium in Arkham. The sanitarium calls Upton to tell him that Derby's "reason has suddenly come back," though upon visiting Upton can see it is not the true personality of Derby, but the person he had encountered on the ride home.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of The Thing on the Doorstep — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Upton is roused from his sleep by a knocking at his door, using Derby's old signal of three-and-two strokes. Upton believes it may be Derby, but opens his door to find a dwarfed, humped messenger concealed under Derby's large coat, carrying a letter from Derby.

The selfish-gene reading of The Thing on the Doorstep makes it less romantic and far more precise. The letter explains that Derby has in fact killed Asenath and buried her body in their cellar. But he should have realized that Asenath's (possibly Ephraim's) soul is partially detached from her body, and that the soul will live on until the body is cremated.

The note implores Upton to go to the sanitarium to kill Derby, who has now been permanently possessed by Ephraim's soul the way he imagines the original Asenath once was.
